paper.title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
paper.abstract: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.

paper.title: Unified CEBRA learns shared neural latents across recordings to map single-neuron contributions to population codes
paper.abstract: Neural computation is thought to rely on distributed populations; however, most single recording samples capture only a fraction of them, and rare cell types may contribute only a small proportion of neurons per session. Pooling many recordings could reveal how these populations encode information, but each recording samples different neurons, so their contributions cannot be easily compared directly. Here we show that recordings can be combined into a single model of all recorded neurons by aligning them with a shared label, used at both training and inference, placing every neuron's contribution to the population code on a common scale. This approach, called Unified CEBRA, retained interpretable task information across recordings in the monkey and mouse sensorimotor cortex, rat hippocampus, and mouse visual cortex. Pooling thousands of excitatory and inhibitory neurons from hundreds of sessions from mouse visual cortex, we found that the neurons that contributed most to the model's readout of visual features were not only the most strongly tuned, but also those that responded more reliably and were less coupled to co-recorded neurons. Unified CEBRA, therefore, can unveil coding principles studied at the population scale with mappable features to individual neurons from sparse, multi-session recordings using our new approach.

paper.title: Hebbian self-organization of monosynaptic reflexes in a biologically realistic multiarticular limb
paper.abstract: Spinal monosynaptic reflexes depend on patterns of connectivity between muscle spindle afferents and motoneurons that should reflect musculoskeletal dynamics. One possibility is that the details of these circuits are specified genetically, but this requires an unlikely coevolution of musculoskeletal and neural elements. Here we show how biomechanical structure can determine the connectivity of self-organized spinal circuits. Using a neuromechanical model combining a multi-joint limb, proprioceptive feedback, and Hebbian plasticity driven by motor babbling, we find that biologically realistic connectivity emerges spontaneously when babbling is neither too sparse nor too frequent. This results in strong homonymous projections, weaker heteronymous projections among functional synergists, and very weak connections among antagonists. This outcome also depends on musculoskeletal morphometry. Heteronymous synergies form when proximal muscles are strongest---the characteristic gradient of mammalian limbs--whereas excessively strong biarticular muscles lead to unphysiological antagonist coupling. The mechanisms differ: homonymous connections arise from direct sensorimotor correlation during fusimotor coactivation by beta motoneurons, while heteronymous connections depend on multi-joint dynamics that emerge only after homonymous reflexes stabilize and increasing muscle strength generates multisegmental motion. Overall, this study provides a mechanistic basis for fetal sensorimotor development and generates testable predictions about the consequences of naturally occurring and experimentally induced variations.
